Deep and constrained digs

Basement excavation, against boundaries and into rock

Bulk and detailed excavation for residential and commercial basements. The deepest and most constrained digs we do: hard against boundaries, often into rock, with a retention system designed by others that the excavation has to work around rather than through. Send the plans and the retention design, and we will price the dig and the spoil.

0456 220 552

Carried out under demolition licence AD214737

Before anything starts

Six things have to be settled first, and not all of them are ours

Most jobs that run late run late on this list rather than on the work itself. Each line says who owns it.

  1. 01

    Geotechnical investigation

    Who You, through a consultant

    Rock level, rock strength and groundwater. Without it the rock is priced on rates rather than a figure, which is honest but less useful to you.

  2. 02

    Retention design

    Who You, through your engineer

    Shoring, piling, anchors or a battered face. This is designed by others and the dig sequence follows it, not the other way round.

  3. 03

    Dilapidation report on neighbours

    Who You, through a consultant

    On a basement against a boundary this protects both sides and is worth doing before, not after.

  4. 04

    Service location and protection

    Who Max, with a locator

    In ground services around the perimeter, found before anything goes down.

  5. 05

    Dewatering approval if needed

    Who You, through your consultant

    If the dig goes below the water table, dewatering has its own approval and its own discharge requirements.

  6. 06

    Truck access and traffic management

    Who Max, with council

    A basement generates far more loads than a site cut, and where they stand is often the constraint.

The detail

Why a basement is not just a deeper hole

  • The retention sets the sequence. Shoring or piling goes in before the dig reaches it, and the excavation follows the design in stages rather than going straight to depth.
  • There is nowhere to put the spoil. On a basement the material leaves as it is generated, so the trucks and the machine have to be sequenced together.
  • Rock arrives partway down. Which means the method and the machine change mid dig, usually from a bucket to a hammer.
  • The neighbours are right there. Vibration, settlement and the condition of the adjoining structure all come into the method before they come into the price.
  • Water is a live risk. A basement that reaches groundwater is a different job, with approvals and discharge requirements attached.
  • Access shrinks as it deepens. Getting the machine out at the end is planned at the start, not discovered at the finish.

Before you book

What people ask about this one

Do you install the shoring?
No. Shoring, piling, anchors and underpinning are engineered and installed by specialists. We excavate in the sequence their design requires, which is a coordination job as much as a digging one.
What if we hit water?
If the dig goes below the water table, dewatering becomes a separate scope with its own approval and discharge requirements. A geotechnical investigation that identifies it beforehand is far cheaper than discovering it with an open hole.
How do you price the rock?
By the cubic metre at a rate agreed before we start, unless a geotechnical report lets us be more specific. Quoting a fixed figure for rock nobody has measured is a guess somebody pays for.
Can you dig right to the boundary?
That depends entirely on the retention design and on what is on the other side. It is an engineering question before it is an excavation one.
How many truck loads is a basement?
More than most people expect, and the number of loads rather than the volume is what the cartage costs. Whether a truck and dog can stand at the kerb changes that number substantially.

Levels, the retention design and a geotechnical report if one exists. Those three decide almost everything about a basement price.
